According to the PUSD website, Witter has been undergoing construction due to major drainage issues. Bothman Construction was contracted for these renovations. While removing the existing track, Bothman found the asphalt beneath the track to be in very poor condition. There was approximately 6000 sq. ft. of substandard asphalt base. However, because of recent heavy rains, Bothman cannot install the entirety of the new track base, and instead will only repair less than 500 sq. ft, said PUSD Director of Facilities and Construction Manager Pete Palmer in an update sent out on Jan. 24. The track and field and lacrosse teams also have also not been able to use Witter for off-season training. articles.text: As we enter April, now designated as Earth Month, there is much to grieve and much to celebrate. On one hand, our planet just experienced its warmest February on record. This was our ninth month in a row with record-breaking temperatures worldwide. On the other hand, we are making unprecedented progress on the long journey away from greenhouse gases. Last year, solar power made up most of the country’s added grid capacity for the first time since World War II. We don’t have to go far to see the shift. Piedmont alone has hundreds of properties with finished solar projects. The origins of Earth Month can be traced to California when Santa Barbara experienced the biggest oil spill in U.S. history in 1969. As the nation watched oil spread over 35 miles of water and witnessed dead animals wash in with the tide, Wisconsin Senator Gaylord Nelson was inspired to take action. Drawing inspiration from student-led anti-war protests, he began planning a nationwide teach-in on college campuses for spring 1970. April 22, the day we still celebrate as Earth Day, was selected to maximize student participation. Over 20 million Americans took part. American environmental consciousness was already growing because of events like the 1962 publication of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring, one of the seminal works on modern environmental science. The first Earth Day unified the fragmented efforts of the nation’s conservationists. In the next few years, the U.S. would not only create the Environmental Protection Agency, but also pass landmark legislation such as the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. This year, I invite everyone to celebrate Earth Month by attending one of these local events: • Earth Day at Chabot Space and Science Center This family-friendly event on April 21 from 10 a.m. - 4 p.m. showcases the many ways local organizations are tackling climate change right here in the Bay, with hands-on activities, guest speakers, and more. Highlights include a field diary hike with Chabot educators, climate storytelling workshops, pollinator-friendly crafts, and an eco-trivia game show. articles.text: Piedmont’s third annual Food Fest is less than three weeks away and the reimagined experience will make good on its promise to offer something for everyone. This year, the multicultural festival will turn Magnolia Avenue into a veritable food boulevard, helping hungry attendees to easily stroll by the many options, making it easy to go back for seconds and even thirds. Additionally, the Food Fest will introduce the Sweet Zone located by the Community Circle, where visitors can sample delicious treats such as gelato, Japanese crepes, and tea cakes while chatting with local non-profits, retailers, and community groups. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year’s lineup of food vendors will include fan favorites such as Robert Dorsey Catering, The Chairman, La Santa Torta, Arthur Mac’s, Satay by the Bay, and Tea on Piedmont, as well as newcomers MOMOlicious, Lahore Di Khushboo, Sunrise Deli, Hila Gelato, and Annie’s T Cakes. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. Visit www.piedmontfoodfest. org for more information on this can’t-miss community experience. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter If you own real property in California, you must pay property taxes twice a year. The second installment of property taxes is due on April 10, next Wednesday. articles.text: Fire Chief Dave Brannigan urges residents to share perspectives on disaster readiness Do you know what you would do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting Fire Chief Dave Brannigan much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the very real possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. articles.text: Last month’s exam on March 9 was the first national administration of the redesigned SAT: an adaptive exam administered on a laptop or tablet. While the core content of the digital SAT is very similar to its predecessor, there are a few major changes: • The digital SAT is now 2 hours and 14 minutes long compared to the old test, which was 3 hours. • The test is adaptive, which means a student’s performance on the first module of each section determines the level of difficulty of the second module of the section. • The reading and writing section has been completely redesigned, and there are no more multi-page passages. • Students can now use a calculator for the entirety of the math section. For students who have been approved for accommodations, the digital SAT can be adapted in a variety of ways. Unlike the SAT, the ACT is not currently going through a major redesign; however, it is piloting the option for computer testing in select locations. ACT scores are accepted at all colleges that accept SAT scores. The new digital SAT comes at a time when colleges are reconsidering their test optional policies. Dartmouth, Yale, and Brown recently announced that they will require standardized test scores for the class of 2029 (current high school juniors) and beyond. After conducting a research study, Dartmouth found that standardized test scores are predictive of academic success at its institution. SAT/ACT scores are also particularly helpful in identifying high-achieving students from under-resourced schools and less advantaged backgrounds. Dartmouth concluded that standardized tests allow them to admit a more diverse and broader range of students, something that is at the forefront of many schools’ minds. Most private universities are committed to a holistic review process. Standardized test scores are a potential opportunity to share more information with a college about a student. As schools gather more information and conduct their own research, it is important to make sure students and families stay informed about testing and other admission requirements as they will surely continue to evolve and can vary school by school. Study Smarter has been providing individualized academic tutoring, test preparation, and college counseling to Piedmont families since 1997. Ariel has worked in undergraduate admissions at both public and private universities. For more information, please visit www.studysmarter.com, email info@studysmarter.com, or call (510) 350-8444.

articles.text: Benicio Perez (left), Emilio Perez and Owen Cain with their collection of signatures in support of their P.E. Teacher Brad Sullivan Piedmont School District’s plan to downsize its staff due to budget concerns is affecting many people. The situation has some students at Wildwood Elementary School unsure of who will teach a favorite class, Physical Education, next year. When a few Wildwood students heard a rumor that their Physical Education teacher, Brad Sullivan, would be leaving, they became upset. When students directly confronted Sullivan about it, he confirmed he likely would not be teaching at Wildwood next year. A pair of brothers, second grader Benicio Perez and fourth grader Emilio Perez, then decided to do something about it. They teamed up with friends, including 4th grader Owen Cain, to collect signatures at recess in support of Mr. Sullivan. With the proposed budget cuts, Wildwood students stand to lose Sullivan, their P.E. teacher, and Louisa Cheung, their veteran Tech teacher next year. The students, along with kindergartener Salvador Perez, recently walked into the office of the Piedmont Post to tell their story about how they acquired the signatures of 111 Wildwood students. Emilio and Owen were inspired by a friend who first made a poster in support of Mr. Sullivan. The poster got left at a friend’s house, but the initiative did not stay at home, the fourth graders brought their concern to the Wildwood blacktop during recess with a student petition. Emilio and Owen received some surprise support for their petition. Unexpectedly a few girls in their class campaigned and they even got some fifth graders to sign. “Pretty much the whole grade likes Mr. Sullivan,” said Emilio. “He makes sure everyone has fun. The previous teachers were nice but didn’t make you try hard, like Mr. Sullivan does.” Younger brother Benicio joined in as well and acquired the signatures of 44 of his classmates – nearly the entire Wildwood 2nd grade – to sign his “Save Mr. Sullivan petition.” Benicio actually performed the task twice, The first petition was done with a yellow marker at recess. When the ink appeared too light to be seen, he got a black pen and got his friends and classmates to sign again. “We were happily surprised. Usually signatures are hard to get,” said Cain. An early version of the kids’ signature sheets was titled “Don’t Fire Mr. Sullivan,” and while that may be what it feels like to the kids, the reality is complex. The district has responded by saying that Sullivan has chosen to resign. Sullivan explained that since he is not tenured, he is still in a probationary period and the district can elect not to bring him back without giving a reason. After two years with the district, a teacher becomes tenured and gains more rights. Sullivan was a long-term substitute with Piedmont Middle School during 2021- 22. Afterwards, his colleagues recommended him for the Wildwood P.E. position, where he is in his second year. “At this point, we’re looking at reducing the number of [P.E.] sections at the high school if we do not have the enrollment,” said Superintendent Hawn. But kids aren’t familiar with compromise, tough decisions and stark realities. One may ask “what’s so special about an elementary P.E. teacher? Can’t anyone teach P.E.?” Sullivan’s students not only acknowledge his charisma and ways of making everyone participate. They also get excited when asked to explain the rules of games Sullivan invented and taught to them. One game is called bucket tag, which combines elements of tag with capture the flag, While recounting the rules of pickle-square and drawing up the field boundary of mat-ball, Sullivan’s students became animated. Sullivan told the Post he loves working in Piedmont and hopes the district will reconsider the planned cut. As it currently stands, the district is likely to move staff around and have multiple P.E. teachers splitting the role with other teaching obligations.
articles.title: Wildwood kids rally to save P.E. teacher from budget cuts

articles.text: Students in kindergarten through 3rd grade will be singing their hearts out this week as each elementary school hosts a Vocal Music Spring concert. The young singers at Beach, Havens and Wildwood have been working hard with vocal music teacher Adrian Behrendt and will celebrate music with a theme of Broadway musicals. Each concert starts at 8:45 a.m. and lasts about 50 minutes. Havens held its concert in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse yesterday morning, Tuesday, April 2. The students in the Beach auditorium will shine brightly tomorrow, Thursday, April 4, and Wildwood students will perform Friday, April 5. “The kids have been working hard with me since January on songs from musicals such as Oliver!, Peter Pan, the King and I, and You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown,” said Behrendt The vocal music spring concerts allow young musicians to step into the role of performer. Although Behrendt expects a lot of his students, he teaches the K-3 graders for only one 40-minute period per week, a significant reduction from the district’s earlier years with a robust music program. “I want them to have fun in concert while striving for their personal best as a musician. I think the community as a whole appreciates the effort the students have put into their performance,” Behrendt said.

articles.text: Staff Photos Gravity Falls TV show creator and PHS alum Alex Hirsch returned to his alma mater last week to serve as a judge at the 55th Annual Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest. After the competition, Hirsch stayed behind to talk with locals in the lobby of the Alan Harvey Theater. Pictured are Sophie Wagganer (left), Alex Hirsch, and Anthony Simons Contestants of the Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest had something extra to be excited about this year. Writer, voice actor, and Piedmont High School (PHS) alum Alex Hirsch agreed to be a celebrity judge for the competition. Hirsch is the creator of the critically-acclaimed Disney TV show Gravity Falls, which besides winning two Emmy Awards, three Annie Awards, and a BAFTA Children’s Award, is also beloved among the student body at Piedmont High School. “We’ve asked him a bunch of times over the years, but there was always a scheduling conflict” said Kathryn Levenson, producer for this year’s contest. “But this year, one of the students, Chaz Amit-Guite, really wanted him to come [...] so I drafted an official-looking email, contacted him, and he said ‘Oh, well, I think I could do that.’” A member of the PHS Class of 2003, Alex Hirsch grew up in Piedmont with his twin sister Ariel. As a junior, he won the Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest in 2002 and earned a chance to perform his bird call on the Tonight Show with David Letterman. Of his call, the Little Blue Heron (Egretta caerulea), Hirsch said the most important parts of his performance were “volume and shamelessness.” During his senior year, Hirsch learned that one of his heroes, Pete Docter of Pixar Animation, would be a judge for the 2003 Bird Calling Contest. Docter, at the time, had just completed Monsters Inc. (2001) to popular and critical success. “I didn’t enter the bird calling contest that second year,” recalled Hirsch. “I really wanted to go to film school for animation and I didn’t know if I was going to get in or not. I was very stressed out, so I coped with that stress by realizing, ‘we’ve got a captive audience here.’” Thus, Hirsch conspired with his classmates Elliot Grossman and Zack Keller to create an animation that would impress Docter. The result was a nine-minute animated short film, Alfred Hitchcluck Presents: Schoolhouse Flock, a story about birds attacking the high school along with a cast of caricatures based on PHS staff, including then vice principal Dennis Creek. The video was shown while the judges decided that year’s winners and received a standing ovation from the audience as well as a mention in the San Francisco Chronicle via its website, SFGate.com. Completing the technically ambitious short by the time of the contest required several all-nighters. articles.text: Piedmont’s team and robot Banshee win top award Banshee (8033) climbs a chain alongside alliance partners in the last seconds of a match. Thirty five members of Highlander Robotics attended the FIRST Robotics Competition’s Orange County Regional last weekend with their robot ‘Banshee’ and won the top judged award, earning their third consecutive qualification to the World Championship to be held in Houston in two weeks. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots built by students in 9th to 12th grade. The competition takes place in in an arena about the size of a basketball court. A new robot, which operates both on its own and with a driver, must be built for each season and local and regional competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. Teams can win awards based on the performance of their robots, on the quality, innovation, and creativity of their designs and the impact they make on their communities. Bids to the World Championship are earned by the captain and first pick of the winning alliance and the winners of the two most prestigious awards, the Impact Award and Engineering Inspiration Award, which the Highlanders received in 2022. The team, attending their second regional of the season and ranked 12th in the state, entered the 48-team event as the favorite. However, after struggling through three different matches where partner robots, which are randomly selected during qualifications, failed to move for some or all of the time they found themselves with a record of five wins and four losses and in 16th place. Even so, they averaged the highest points in the tournament and in the draft preceding the double-elimination playoffs were the first selection of the tournament by the first seed captain “Robot Dolphins from Outer Space” from Dana Point. The three-team alliance was completed with 16th pick, Team Sprocket from Diamond Bar. In the first round of playoffs the alliance won, setting a tournament high score of 137-61. In their second match however, Banshee malfunctioned during the self-driving period, moving at full speed into a steel truss and afterwards had difficulty picking up game pieces. The alliance lost to the fourth seed captained by Nomad from Escondido. In the lower bracket, despite a rapid set of repairs performed by the Highlanders pit crew, Banshee continued to behave erratically and struggled through two more wins 97-79 and 95-58 largely due to the strength of the Dolphin’s robot, Siren. Finally, in the semi-finals, the Highlanders’ alliance lost a second time to Nomad and finished third overall. In the awards ceremony the Highlanders were awarded Scouting Lead Cassie Colby works with her counterpart to choose a third alliance Partner before playoffs. Mechanical Lead Ayaan Jajodia repairs the robot Banshee between matches.
articles.title: Highlander Robotics qualifies for Worlds for 3rd time

articles.text: Vaughn Khouri, Vice Captain of Highlander Robotics, has been selected as a FIRST Dean’s List Finalist and will represent California at the World Championship in Houston later this month. FIRST founder Dean Kamen sponsors The Dean’s List award to highlight outstanding 10th and 11th grade student leaders involved in FIRST’s international robotics competitions. Nominees have demonstrated a commitment to promoting STEM in their communities and shown personal technical expertise and accomplishment. Khouri’s nomination cited his volunteer work mentoring other robotics teams, building STEM curriculum through a non-profit he founded for that purpose, and growing training programs within Highlander Robotics. “FIRST has become a huge part of my life and a lot of what I do within it is beyond our team” said Khouri. “The award seems to recognize that alongside my leadership on 8033 and it feels incredible to receive it.” Similar to the National Merit Scholarship Award, there are three levels of FIRST Dean’s List Award students. Semi-Finalists Vaughn Khouri and Lewy Seiden, both juniors at Piedmont High School, were nominated by the Highlander Robotics team 8033. After interviews, two Finalists are selected across all teams in a regional robotics competition. Khouri was named at the Orange County Regional out of semi-finalists from 48 teams. His nomination will now advance to Houston where 10 Dean’s List Winners will be selected from roughly 100 Finalists on April 19. “Vaughn is the real deal,” said Highlanders Lead Mentor Natalia Feretti. “He has the vision, the skills and the leadership to be a strong advocate for quality STEM education in our community. We are all so proud of him and can’t wait to see what he’ll do with that transformative power.” FIRST’s most prestigious award, the Impact Award, which honors the team that best represents a model for other teams to emulate and embodies the mission of FIRST. The judges cited the use of their skills to support Oakland School District’s Special Education department, their free release of a scouting application used by hundreds of other teams to track robot performance at competitions, and the number of communities they touched with teammates in 17 schools over 11 districts. Banshee was operated by Vaughn Khouri and Max Seiden and supported by drive coach Justin Green, technician Alex Gish, and human player Chloe Kessinger. Highlander Robotics was founded in 2019 by brothers Henry and Charlie Lambert and is composed of 62 students from 17 high schools around the area. They work from the Mary G Ross Engineering Lab at Piedmont High School. For more information, visit the team on its website: frc8033.com. ®

articles.text: Highlanders beat Yellowjackets 12-10 in Berkeley Ruby Guzdar scored four goals in a big win over Berkeley. Piedmont’s girls’ lacrosse team is rolling on a four-game winning streak following a narrow 12-10 victory over Berkeley, a Western Alameda County Conference foe, on Thursday, March 28. With a 9-2 overall record and undefeated at 4-0 against league teams, the Highlanders are firmly in first-place with four games left in the regular season. Ruby Guzdar continued to lead the team with four goals. She earlier scored seven goals against Bishop O’Dowd and five in a victory over College Park. Chloe Graham notched a hat trick with three goals, and Laurel Bentley helped put the game away with w critical goal with five minutes left. Piedmont has one match before spring break at San Marin this Thursday. They return on April 16 for the start of three games in three days starting with Miramonte at home, followed by Granada at home the next day, and will close the regular season at Newark Memorial. The Highlanders are set to enter the WACC Tournament on Wednesday, April 26 with as the No. 1 seed with the championship round being hosted at Berkeley two days later. 12-10 win at Berkeley Piedmont carried a 4-3 lead through the first quarter and went up 7-5 at halftime. But Berkeley went on a wild five-goal scoring run in the third quarter to capture the lead at 10-9 entering the fourth. However, the Highlander defense kept Berkeley scoreless in the final quarter and scored three goals to secure the win. In the first quarter, Piedmont’s Friedie Schickedanz scored the game’s opening goal after 45 seconds, but Berkeley tied on their next possession and went ahead with 7:33 on the clock. The matched waged on scoreless until Guzdar got her first goal with 2:28 remaining. Chloe Graham then put PHS up with around 1:20 on the clock, then Hallie Burden made it 4-2 on the very next possession just 20 seconds later. But Berkeley got one back with eight seconds left, 4-3. Guzdar scored again quickly in the second quarter on a run from the left side on Piedmont’s opening possession, but Berkeley quickly answered less than a minute later and then tied 5-5 with around seven minutes on the Staff Photos clock. Guzdar, once again, put PHS ahead with around 3:30 left, then Schickedanz made a play to score a couple of minutes later to make it 7-5 going into half. In the third, Graham made it 8-5 after around four minutes of action, then Burden quickly added their ninth goal. But from there, Berkeley went on a five goal scoring run to end the quarter leading 10-9. Guzdar tied things up at 10-10 with 9:55 left in the game on another rocket into the net. Slightly over a minute later, Graham put Piedmont ahead 11-10. Then with around five minutes left, Laurel Bentley scored to clinch the victory. Final stats: Guzdar had four goals, one assist, one ground ball and won one draw control. Graham had three goals while Schickedanz had two. Burden had two goals, three ground balls, and won four draw controls. Bentley scored once. Hailey Marshbrun won five draw controls and scooped one ground ball. Goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter had five saves. NEXT UP Piedmont (9-2 overall, 4-0 league) heads to San Marin in Novato on Thursday, April 4. Chloe Graham scored three goals against Berkeley. Laurel Bentley scored the final goal to help clinch the win over Berkeley.

articles.text: Piedmont’s softball team looks strong in its first eight games of the season, building a 6-2 record thus far. Over their last three games, Piedmont has scored 45 runs and allowed five. They recently defeated Healdsburg 19-1 at Witter softball field on Monday, April 1. They beat San Lorenzo on the road 15-3 on Thursday, March 28, and bashed Tennyson 11-1 in Hayward on Tuesday, March 26. “We’re trying to put together some wins. We’re a young team, we have only six girls returning from last year and have five new players,” said coach Gene Denard, “Learning the game of softball is tough and sometimes and it shows. We’re just going day by day.” It’s been a big start to the season for several returners from last year’s team. Leading the team in hitting is junior Angelina Wu with a sterling .632 batting average with 12 hits in 19 at bats, including 19 runs out of the leadoff position, 13 stolen bases, and 11 walks. Junior Miya Fujimoto is also swinging the bat with a big .526 average with 10 hits in 19 at bats, a double, triple, 13 runs scored and 13 RBIs in the three-spot. She’s also drawn eight walks. Both Wu and Fujimoto carry the innings for PHS’ pitching staff. Fujimoto, who usually lines up at shortstop as the team’s best infielder, is 2-1 and has thrown 21.1 innings with 2.625 ERA, 39 strikeouts. Wu is 3-1 in 18.2 innings pitched with an identical 2.625 ERA and 21 strikeouts. “A lot of things fall on Fuji and Angelina. We’re trying not to give them too many innings just yet. I don’t even think Miya is really getting into her groove yet,” Denard said. Emerging in the starting lineup is junior Samantha Ronin, hitting .350 with seven hits and the team’s only home run, including nine RBIs, nine runs scored, and seven stolen bases. She can also contribute on the mound with three innings pitched. 19-1 over Healdsburg PHS opened with a bang, scoring 11 runs in the bottom of the first inning, scored twice in the second, once in the third, and another five in the bottom of the fourth—activating the 10-run rule after the top of the fifth. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team suffered a rough 3-0 loss to Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division opponent Alameda on Thursday, March 28 by scores of 25-20, 25-14, 25-15 at Binks Rawlings Gym. It’s been a tough start for the squad this year after losing all but two starters from last year’s roster – Shunji Higashi and John Champion. Last year’s team was a big part of redeveloping boys’ volleyball at PHS after the sports’ 20-year absence at the school. PHS is still about middle of the pack at 4-6 in the WACC and must take four of its final six matches in order to qualify for North Coast Section for a third consecutive year. “We’re just trying to have fun and make sure the kids keep coming back. It’s been sad to see the drop off from last year. We’re 4-6 in league and have beaten the teams I think we needed to. When we go against those bigger schools, those teams have a lot of players who do club. We only have a few kids playing club, so players are learning this game for the first time,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Still, Cardenas sees bright spots, including senior Spencer Sorensen-Wald. He just started playing volleyball competitively for the first time after being a pole vaulter on the track and field team last year. He’s Piedmont’s primary outside hitter opposite of Champion. “It’s a great community; I love all the guys, but it hurts when we lose. I just started playing this year. I did a couple of open gyms, but not much after that. It’s a lot of technique and mine may not be the best, but I’m learning as I go,” Sorensen-Wald said. Piedmont will have a chance to rebound at Encinal on Thursday, April 4 for its final match before spring break, then they’ll return on April 15 against Berkeley. 3-0 loss to Alameda Piedmont lost in three straights sets by scores of 25-20, 25-14, 25-15. Last year’s team was a big part of redeveloping boys’ volleyball at PHS after the sports’ 20-year absence at the school. When we go against those bigger schools, those teams have a lot of players who do club. We only have a few kids playing club, so players are learning this game for the first time,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Still, Cardenas sees bright spots, including senior Spencer Sorensen-Wald. He just started playing volleyball competitively for the first time after being a pole vaulter on the track and field team last year. He’s Piedmont’s primary outside hitter opposite of Champion. “It’s a great community; I love all the guys, but it hurts when we lose. I just started playing this year. articles.text: Museum member previews this Thursday & Friday The Legion of Honor museum in San Francisco will open its newest exhibition, Japanese Prints in Transition: From the Floating World to the Modern World, on Saturday, April 6. The two-part exhibition will feature permanent collection works from the Achenbach Foundation for Graphic Arts that haven’t been displayed in over a decade, highlighting the Meiji era (1868–1912), Japan’s period of modernization and exchange with other nations. The period marks when Japan’s shogun was overthrown marking the end of feudal military rule in the Asian country. The period also displays a shift in Japanese art and especially printmaking. Scenic views, like oceans and valleys, dominated prints for over a century but were replaced with vivid images of Western architecture and technology. The exhibition highlights the work of Tsukioka Yoshitoshi, who worked in both pre-and postMeiji era. A museum member preview takes place Thursday, April 4 and Friday, April 5. A Japanese Prints in Transition donor reception will be held on Thursday, April 11, from 7 to 9 p.m. The exhibition is on display at Legion of Honor through August 18. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/japanese-prints.
articles.title: Japanese Prints exhibit opens at Legion of Honor this Saturday

articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra will perform its Spring Concert on Saturday, April 27; at 7:30 p.m. at First Church Berkeley, 2345 Channing Way. The program of music includes Gershwin’s An American In Paris (1928), Stravinsky’s’ Firebird Suite (1945), and select chamber music pieces. Tickets are $20 General, and free for students who register at the ticket site. For advance tickets see http://data.ypsomusic.org/ tickets. This year, YPSO celebrates its 87th season and Maestro David Ramadanoff’s 35th season as Music Director/Conductor. He will be conducting approximately 100 young musicians who range in age from 11 to 21, and hail from Bay Area cities from Napa to Pleasanton. Starting this season, YPSO offers free admission to youth 13 and under accompanied by an adult, and to high school and college students with valid ID. YPSO asks that all concert goers, including students, please register on their ticket site, even if some tickets are free, in order to maintain appropriate seating capacity counts. Program The Spring Concert will feature two iconic pieces, George Gershwin’s An American in Paris and Igor Stravinsky’s The Firebird Suite. In addition, the concert will showcase select chamber music pieces performed by YPSO chamber ensembles. American in Paris is a symphonic tone poem that captures the spirit of Paris in the 1920s. Known for its jazzy rhythms and colorful orchestration, the piece is a vibrant portrayal of the bustling streets, Parisian nightlife, and the joie de vivre of the city. The performance will feature the percussion section with taxi horns, the woodwind section with bluesy saxophones, as well as the brass section with a spotlight on trumpets. Stravinsky’s 1945 version of The Firebird Suite is a ballet suite derived from his larger work, “The Firebird.” Composed for the 1910 Paris season of Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russe, the suite includes some of the most memorable music from the ballet. Visit the online auction website at ypso2024.ggo.bid. The auction will feature a variety of goods and services donated by YPSO families and local businesses. They include wine tastings, outdoor adventures, and homemade meals, Proceeds support YPSO’s orchestra education program, scholarships for students in need, and the upcoming tour to Japan this summer. This annual fundraiser is a vital part of supporting YPSO’s music education program - ensuring that no student is left behind. articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, likely the best-known and most successful Spanish filmmaker of the last three decades. His most memorable film in the U.S. was Volver (Return), and starred Penelope Cruz, considered Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. As she is gradually pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity the film takes on a noirish tone, moving from 2008 to 1994 The film is completely taken with the transformative face of Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like we are lookmatic westerns. Penélope Cruz and José Luis Gómez in Broken Embraces ing at a Vogue fashion layout, so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance. Perhaps it is because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices; the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the audience is not interested in knowing about the motivations of the characters. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s new animated movie Soul Soul is an animated fantasy/ comedy produced by Pixar-Disney Animation Studios and directed by Pete Docter and Kemp Powers. The filmography of Pixar-Disney is extraordinary and has demonstrated a remarkable consistency in its ability to create magical entertainment for youngsters, examples being the Toy Story franchise, Inside Out, Up, Coco, Lightyear, and Wall-E. Soul opens with the sounds of off-key, discordant band music and quickly cuts to a New York City middle school cluster of kids all playing a variety of instruments, led by their tall, lanky music teacher, Joe Gardner (Jamie Foxx). The look on his face tells all. He’s cringing while the kids are doing their best to play a marching song that is unrecognizable. Finally, class is over and as Joe prepares to leave he is stopped by the principal and told that he has been hired permanently. Unexpectedly, Joe’s reaction is ambivalent. We soon learn that his passion is to play gigs at jazz clubs rather than teach. Shortly after leaving school he gets a phone call from a former student, Lamont “Curley” Baker (Quesrlove), who remembers Joe’s love of playing jazz. He’s heard of an opportunity to audition as a pianist with the iconic saxophonist Dorothea Williams (Angela Bassett). He goes and lets ‘er rip. Dorothea is impressed and hires him on the spot. His longedfor opportunity has arrived. Joe leaves the audition with his head in the clouds, oblivious to the crowded streets of New York. Paying no attention to where he is walking, he falls into an open manhole. Before continuing with the journey of Joe Gardner, it’s impossible not to comment on the animation created by Pixar in acts one and three. It’s astonishingly good – as close to photography as can be imagined and so good it’s almost surreal. NYC comes alive, people, cars, buses, all viewed through the lens of the animators’ talented imagination. Pixar has a long history of knowing its audience, those youngsters who stand ready to suspend their disbelief. But then there’s Joe at the bottom of the manhole. And thus begins act two. The narrative cuts to a disembodied Joe (the soul of Joe) on a crowded moving walkway, surrounded by tiny blue blobs headed to the “Great Beyond.” Wait. Joe died as a result of the fall? Do important characters ever die in cartoons? In Soul, apparently the answer is yes. And rather abruptly the story shifts to a place in which Joe is not a hip jazz musician or a music teacher; instead, he’s a fuzzy, blue image of his former self with only his familiar hat and glasses. He really doesn’t want to go to any beyond, and definitely not to a place called the “Great Before.” While possible to barely track the story from this point on, it loses its mojo. Heaven (a word never mentioned in the story) is not a gig that Joe wants any part of. There are strange denizens and other wordly counselors all named Jerry. Keep in mind that in the world of Pixar’s audience, death and what’s beyond is way out of their wheelhouse. Why include the metaphysical scenes at all? You might ask if Joe find his way back to NYC? Or wake up in a hospital? Yes and no. Will he make his way back to the piano? I don’t want to be a spoiler, so I’ll stop here. But I did miss the Joe who was introduced at the outset. He’s a sweet character with a dream, a guy in search of a different life, who ultimately learns the lesson that he should follow his passion, which is to play jazz. He will thereby find that life can be remarkable. Soul. Directed by Pete Docter and Kemp Powers. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Jamie Foxx, Phylicia Rashad, Angela Bassett. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated PG. Released in 2020. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/Disney+.

Harvey Dong of Eastwind Books sold almost all 100 books he brought. Wong read excerpts from his most recent book, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America, and answer questions posed by Dong and audience members, many of whom patiently waited in a long line for Wong to sign. “I felt so uplifted by their presence and support,” Wong said. “A classmate from elementary school whom I hadn’t seen in many decades showed up and bought 4 books. We exchanged warm, if brief, greetings, then Bill Wong signs copies of his newest book, Sons of Chinatown: A Memoir Rooted in China and America. we texted one another. He called me yesterday from his home in Vacaville and told me how he learned of my event. His sister lives in Piedmont and she saw the articles [in the Post] which she sent to her brother, my old friend. He drove down from Vacaville just to see me and buy my books.” Wong said. Copies of the book are available at www.williamgeewong. com for access to Temple University Press. articles.text: Where is the best place to hear a concert? Some people like large auditoriums and big name stars who frequently “phone in“ their performances. Do you think that Frederick Chopin would sound good under these circumstances? I don’t think so. He was always at his best performing for an intimate crowd. I think Frederick Chopin would have loved our Piedmont Center for the Arts. You can be sure that private concerts in Chopin’s time included delicious refreshments as well as lively conversation. These are some of the benefits we get at the concerts at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. That’s the way it was last Saturday evening, March 30, when the members of the Temescal Quartet were joined by pianistCarl Blake. To make matters even better, the concert was free, and there was an excellent catered reception after the concert. I arrived early and heard the musicians in lively discussion. All five of them are longtime friends. Part of the conversation was where to set up. At the Piedmont Center for the Arts, it really doesn’t matter because every seat is a good seat. Another good thing is that the acoustics are lively. As the audience assembled, it was quite clear that they were part of the performance. It is always gratifying to see young people at concerts. What a joy to see so many young kids enjoying the music. All aspects for the concert were a combination of formal and informal. The concert was entitled “Taking flight – a fugal adventure.” Every aspect of the programming showed great intelligence. The entire first half contained pieces which somehow flew under the guise of the word “Fugue” (meaning to pursue). Most of the selections were short, but they formed an impressive unity. “Contrapunctus 1” from the Art of the Fugue by Bach and the finale from Haydn’s String Quartet Op. 20, No. 6 served as warm-ups. delssohn’s Scherzo Fugue, the quartet’s emotional energy really sprang to life. Released in 1963 and directed by Terence Young, From Russia with Love saw Sean Connery’s second outing in the role he would play seven times. In this adventure he battles SMERSH, the evil multinational organization bent on sowing disruption and seizing power, headed by the slyly malevolent Ernst Stavro Blofeld, who strokes a purring cat while he plans mayhem. Connery is abetted by Danielle Bianchi as the “Bond girl,” Bernard Lee as M, and Robert Shaw, Pedro Armanderiz, and Lotte Lenya as the assassin with a knife in her shoe. If you’re anything like me, a ray of sunshine in the garden has me pulling out my collection of seed packets, ready to get sowing. There are so many ways to start seeds and I’ve tested a lot of them. After my fair share of fruitful and failed attempts, here are a few tricks I’ve learned. First, start with seeds that are no more than three years old for the strongest germination. Starting seeds is an act of patience, so I don’t want to take my chances with seeds that may be past their prime and fail to germinate. Head online or to the local nursery to gather your favorite 2024 seed varieties. Buying seed packets rather than seed starts offers much more choice of unique varieties - like Barry’s Crazy cherry tomatoes or Dragon’s Tongue bush beans! Second, choose a high-quality potting soil to create the ideal growing conditions for your seeds. You can purchase E.B. Stone’s 420 Potting Mix which is stocked at the Grand Lake Ace Garden Center and most local nurseries. Ideally, you’re looking for a mix that provides moisture retention, like coconut coir or peat moss. Try earthworm castings as a source of organic matter to provide beneficial microbes and bacteria. articles.text: A good turnout of 33 walkers and two K-9 best friends showed up for last week’s Walking on Wednesdays stroll. The Piedmont Heritage Tree Program was created in 2018 by the City Council on a recommendation from the Park Commission. It has designated 28 Piedmont trees as “Heritage Trees.” The intent of the program is to recognize noteworthy, distinctive trees in Piedmont city parks or open spaces, encourage residents to visit City parks and open spaces, and promote the study of nature. Last spring, the walkers nominated the mulberry trees in front of the Piedmont Play School at Hampton Park as Heritage Trees, and with the help of the tots at the school who also proposed it, they won. The walkers have proposed another tree this year, and the winners will be announced by Arbor Day, April 26. The walkers decided last week to see some past winners. Getting started was easy as they looked up at the trees that surround the Exedra Plaza. This grove of 10 Highland poplars are Heritage Trees. They are a hybrid of two North American plain poplars that are native to the Northern Hemisphere. The walkers then made their way to City Hall to see a group of Evergreen dogwoods at its entrance. These trees are native to Bhutan, China, on the Himalayas’ eastern edge. Then it was down Vista Avenue to Hillside to see the stately palm trees at the Recreation Center. These trees are known as Canary Island date palms or pineapple palms. They are native to the Canary Islands off the coast of Northwestern Africa. Jim Kellogg said this is a popular palm species because its trunk doesn’t grow large and the canopy of palms at its top have a uniform shape. The group then went to the tot lot behind the Exedra to see a Coast live oak grouping, and continuing on, Coast live oaks on the path to Bushy Dell Creek. A large, twisting Coast live oak that has been used for family photos is a Heritage Tree too. These oaks are native to California’s central valleys, as far north as Mendocino County, and as far south as Baja California in Mexico. In front of the Community Hall is a Yulan magnolia, native to central and eastern China. It and produces stunning white flowers in the spring. Other Heritage Trees nearby are Japanese maples, native to Japan, Korea, China, eastern Mongolia, and southeast Russia, and a group of Akebono cherry trees from Japan. Near the Community Hall is the Coast Redwood that serves as Piedmont’s holiday tree in December. The walkers continued to Guilford Road and Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa Road the walkers saw another large Coast redwood Heritage Tree. This specific tree once marked the entrance to the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls, Piedmont’s first school, which opened in 1913. The walkers went up Requa, down Highland, and up Wildwood Avenue. This two block section of Wildwood was originally lined with large, stately and colorful American elms, but they died from Dutch elm disease. Thy were replaced with colorful but smaller trees, Autumn Blaze maples. The ones on Wildwood are Heritage Trees. Wild Autumn Blaze maples are found in eastern North America where the parent species overlap. Just off Wildwood is the Hall Fenway and a grove of European white birches that are native to Europe and parts of Asia. The walkers went on to Crocker Park looking for a Copper beech. It is deep purple in the spring and turns to a coppery hue in the autumn. Not all trees in the park had their leaves, and the group wasn’t sure which one was the Heritage Tree. The walkers continued to Hampton Park so see the mulberry trees at Piedmont Play School. These trees are known as white mulberry, common mulberry and silkworm mulberry. The species is native to China and India and is widely cultivated elsewhere including in the United States, Mexico, Australia, Kyrgyzstan, Argentina, Turkey, and Iran. Cut or peel the rinds from the grapefruit and orange, making sure to remove the white pith, which is bitter. Slice crosswise into 1/4-inch rounds. Cut each round into large bite-sized pieces. Transfer to a large salad bowl. 2. Cut the avocadoes in half lengthwise and remove the pit - carefully. Cut into lengthwise quarters then slice across each quarter into 1/2-inch pieces. articles.text: Shelagh (Phibbs) Udovch, an active member of the Piedmont community for 47 years, passed away on March 21, 2024, from complications related to dementia. She was 84 years old. Shelagh was born in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 1939, and graduated from Potchefstroom High School for Girls in 1957. She worked as a bookkeeper at Rustenberg Farm in Stellenbosch before sailing from Cape Town to Southampton, England, in 1960. Getting her first taste of travel, she decided to keep going. She sailed to Canada with friends, and then drove across the country during the depths of winter in a Volkswagen Beetle. She settled temporarily in Vancouver, where she worked as a Secretary to the Vice President of Engineering at the B.C. Telephone company. Upon visiting San Francisco in 1963, she was offered employment as a receptionist at the South African Consulate and eventually became Secretary to the Consul-General. While working at the Consulate, she met her husband, Frank Udovch, on the tennis courts of San Francisco. Playing tennis was to become one of their favorite pastimes. Shelagh enjoyed not only the competitive and social aspects of tennis, but also the obligatory cold beer after a tough match. When her sons were born, tennis remained a central part of her life, and the Udovch family could often be seen playing family doubles on the Piedmont tennis courts or at the Berkeley Tennis Club. Shelagh Udovch passed away on March 21, 2024. She was 84. Shelagh became the first locally hired staff member to join the Scottish Development Agency. Over the next 22 years, she helped multiple directors from Scotland transition to life in the local office and in the Bay Area. Her networking skills were legendary; she continually had to reorder her business cards, which she would distribute to any interested riders that she picked up from the Casual Carpool line on Oakland Avenue on her daily commute to San Mateo. Mere days after she and Frank moved to Piedmont in 1977, two Piedmont moms rang the Udovch doorbell, and recruited Shelagh for the Beach School mother’s Club (now the BPO) treasurer position. She happily obliged. As time went by, she continued her volunteerism and community involvement with the Piedmont Community Church, Dress Best for Less, the Red Cross, and League of Women Voters. When the Piedmont Post first started, Shelagh agreed to spearhead advertising sales, selling ad space to local businesses. Shelagh’s picture was often found in the early Post editions’ “Where in the World” section, featuring shots of her many travels around the world. Shelagh was fun-loving and spontaneous. Whether driving her youngest son Justin down to Mexico on a surfing trip or traveling solo to Turkey, she was always game for a new adventure. When her husband died suddenly in 1999, she began recruiting new travel companions. She loved to host parties and share a glass of Chardonnay with anyone who was available. All who knew her would not soon forget her unabashed physical affection and her trademark move of beginning a dinner-party conversation with a potentially shocking opening line. Shelagh is survived by her sons Peter (Leila Hebshi) Udovch of Piedmont and Justin (Joy) Udovch of South Kona, Hawaii; and four grandchildren. She is also survived by sisters Sandra Rickwood and Evelynne Gunn of Surrey, UK. She was preceded in death by her sister Karin Cockroft, and her brother Owen Phibbs, both of South Africa. articles.text: Wayne Batavia, a lifelong Bay Area resident and longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on March 27, 2024. Born Wayne Ellis Batavia on August 31, 1954, he was the youngest child of George and Katherine Batavia. He attended Skyline High School where he was Student Body President, then University of California in Berkeley where he majored in Business with a concentration in Real Estate. He spent one year away from the Golden State to earn a Masters of Science degree in Real Estate at the University of Wisconsin in Madison. He soon returned with his beloved dog, Shade and began a career spanning 30 years as a Real Estate Developer and Consultant. It brought him a great sense of accomplishment and joy. Wayne met his wife Melissa “Missy” Kane on a blind date and they were married in 1981. They have two children, Julia and Margaret (Colleen), with whom Wayne enjoyed spending as much time as possible: whether walking the dog, playing sports, watching movies, going camping, or eating dinner together every night after he got home from work. Wayne loved his family, and spending time with them was his greatest passion. Over the years, Wayne enjoyed being an active member at Temple Sinai in Oakland, and with the greater Jewish community. He was a member of two wine tasting groups, a softball player as well as coach, an avid skier Wayne Batavia died on March 27. He was 69. and cyclist, and a proud Porsche driver. Above all he was a steadfast friend to the many people who loved him, and whom he loved in return. He is survived by Melissa, his wife of 42 years, and daughters Julia and Margaret (Colleen). He is also survived by older siblings Leslie (Stan) DeLugach and Clyde (Gail) Batavia. To honor Wayne and with a nod to his untimely death brought on by a long battle with Lewy Body Dementia, the family requests that memorial donations be made to the Brain Support Network for the advancement of research in brain diseases. The website is www.brainsupportnetwork.org.

articles.text: At its March meeting the Piedmont Beautification Foundation (PBF) joined the bandwagon gaining steam to reforest Piedmont with native plants, neighborhood by neighborhood. Among the reasons for this ambitious effort is climate change, which seems to be more concerning with each passing month. Many trees and other plants which thrived in a moderate climate with plenty of rain every winter are suffering and dying in our increasingly hot, windy weather. Two recent examples of this new effort include: 1) the Park Commission spent a day at Bushy Dell Creek planting riparian native plants donated by Watershed Nursery thanks to Tom and Jane Kelly of Greens at Work. 2) Piedmont Garden Club commemorated it’s 100th Birthday with a $10,000 donation to the City. The funds will be used to install native plants near the Firehouse at City Hall. Next is the much-anticipated decision as to what to plant to replace the iconic Sequoia gigantea in the traffic circle at the Mountain and Bellevue intersection. This redwood tree stood tall in this intersection for generations, even serving as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 1920s and 1930s (stopped by the onset of WWII). Showing grave danger of toppling, this tree was removed last fall. At its March meeting the Park Commission approved the recommendation of the City staff and supported by PBF to replace that tree with an Island Oak (Quercus tomontella), a tree indigenous to California (especially the Channel Islands) and regarded as likely to thrive in a small traffic island that has no regular source of water. PBF will undertake a campaign to raise funds to select a good specimen of Island Oak. Campaign proceeds will help refurbish the traffic circle with suitable landscaping, install a plaque commemorating the Sequoia, contribute to the cost of hand watering through the City’s landscape maintenance contract, and provide care for the Island Oak for its first two years. After that time the tree should thrive on its own. Representatives of PBF plan to visit nearby neighbors to solicit funds for the project. PBF’s main Spring project will be on a much larger scale: a campaign to reforest Piedmont neighborhoods. A map of the City will be marked with areas where reforestation is needed. This will include parks, civic areas, traffic circles, tree-lined streets, and other appropriate spots. The emphasis will be to replace trees that are no longer surviving in our increasingly harsh climate with trees indigenous to California that are likely to thrive going forward. PBF’s Spring Brochure (to be mailed in early May) will show various neighborhoods to which gifts may be targeted. PBF and the City will first aim to reforest Dracena Park, where the need for new trees is most urgent. Donors who wish to contribute to an alternative area where reforestation is needed will be able to do so. This exciting new campaign will be known as “Reforesting Piedmont Neighborhood by Neighborhood.” The community is encouraged to look for PBF’s Spring brochure which will include details on how to give our City a beautiful, new and greener look. Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s mission, in partnership with the City, is to provide a safe, sustainable and beautiful community. The foundation is comprised of eight trustees from the City and Piedmont Garden Club, and 26 advisors from the community at large. To learn more about Piedmont Beautification Foundation, please visit https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation.org/.

articles.text: White Elephant Sale volunteers reveal the amount of money raised at last year’s Sale – $2,650,000 – the largest in the history of Oakland Museum. This year’s annual White Elephant Sale, a major fundraiser for Oakland Museum of California, raised more than $2.652,000 – a record high in the museum’s history. The sale was held five weeks in February and March. Organized and presented by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, it is the largest annual fundraising event benefiting the museum. A substantial portion of the proceeds supports exhibitions, programming, and operations each year. An army of volunteers staff the different departments in the WES warehouse, a large building on Lancaster Street in East Oakland. At an event where the total amount raised was revealed, each department recited a little bit about the items they sold, then the volunteers turned over their cards to show the total dollar amount. In a skit, volunteers on the right side of a lineup of seven people shoed the number 2, so that the total amount was revealed in reverse order. “We were so excited to welcome shoppers back to the warehouse for our 65th White Elephant Sale, and continue our mission to support OMCA,” said Marge Harvey, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. “I’m so proud of our Board and our dedicated volunteers for their commitment to this Oakland tradition.” “We are extremely grateful for the extraordinary commitment of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board to OMCA throughout the past 65 years,” said Museum Director and CEO Lori Fogarty. “As the single largest donor to OMCA, the Women’s Board and their White Elephant Sale are absolutely essential to the success of the Museum. We extend our heartfelt thanks to the leadership of the Women’s Board and the hard work of hundreds of volunteers who make the White Elephant Sale possible each year.”

He would go on to work on shows like Cartoon Network’s Marvelous Misadventures of Flapjack, and the Disney Channel series Fish Hooks before creating Gravity Falls in 2012. Students at this year’s bird calling contest were aware of Hirsch’s presence. After one performance, a student on the way off the stage flashed a triangle gesture around his eye toward the judges table, a reference to a fan-favorite character on Gravity Falls, Bill Cipher. Others whispered excitedly to one another in the audience about his presence between acts. After the contest, Hirsch set up a small table in the lobby of the Alan Harvey Theater where adults and children alike came to talk with him and get items signed—a mixture of contest programs and Gravity Falls memorabilia. The atmosphere was warm and informal as Hirsch answered questions from fans and doled out life advice to young animation hopefuls. Hirsch said that he doesn’t regret skipping class to work on “Alfred Hitchcluck Presents...,” because it led to a fruitful animation career that he loves dearly. “So remember that, kids. Drop out of school and you’ll be a big success!” laughed Hirsch.
